transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-21
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (Cascade - Head of Platform), Ethan Chen (Cascade - SRE), Liam O'Rourke (Cascade - CTO)

Summary: discovery focused on reliability/fallback policies, multi-region routing, SLAs and Private vs Dedicated tradeoffs. Customer asked about automated fallbacks, KV cache behavior across regions, encryption and KMS, and what Redwood's observable signals and runbooks look like.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey folks, thanks for carving out time. Jordan from Redwood, joined by Priya our solutions engineer. How's everyone?
[00:06] Maria: Hi, good thanks. We've been looking at Redwood for a few weeks. Want to see how you handle reliability — we have strict uptime and geo rules.
[00:12] Priya: Awesome. Today we can walk through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for reliability use cases, failover patterns, and some example policies. We'll also capture next steps for a benchmark.
[00:20] Liam: Quick context — Cascade runs a unified inference layer used by search, recommendations, and a new real-time feature for customers. Latency SLO is 150ms p95 for interactive routes, and availability needs to be 99.95 across primary regions. We also have strict EU data residency for a subset of traffic.
[00:35] Ethan: And we care about incident tolerance — if a region goes down we need automatic fallback to a secondary region without big latency spikes, also we want predictable cost if we do cross-region failover.

[01:02] Priya: Great. High level: Hosted is the easiest — Redwood runs the control plane, we provide multi-region endpoints and can route by region, latency or cost. For Dedicated you get a reserved GPU pool in a region, stronger throughput guarantees and isolation. Private is where the control plane is customer-managed (VPC/on-prem) for compliance. Each mode has different tradeoffs for failover.
[01:30] Jordan: I want to call out two things up front — automated fallbacks and model variant routing. We do prefix caching and KV cache which helps warm the tails. In multi-region failover we can route to a compatible model variant in a nearby region and preserve cache hits where possible, but there are cold-start considerations.

[02:05] Maria: Let's walk through a scenario: EU region goes down. We want traffic to fail to EU-proximate region, keep data residency for EU-only traffic where required, but for non-restricted traffic we can fail to US. How would that look?
[02:20] Priya: (short pause) Two approaches — policy-based routing or weighted failover. Policy-based: tag routes as EU-resident and set hard block to not leave EU. Weighted failover: prefer EU pool, if latency/health fails to meeting threshold, fail to secondary. For Hosted customers we expose routing policies in Console and API. For Dedicated we can run a secondary dedicated pool in another region or configure cross-region routing to a compatible Hosted pool.
[02:50] Ethan: How fast is the failover and what's the expected latency bump? If we're routed to US it's gotta stay within SLO or we need the app to degrade gracefully.
[03:00] Priya: Failover detection is based on health checks and latency monitors — can be tuned to 30s-2m detection windows. Cold-start overhead to a new pool depends on model size and whether there's KV/prefix caching. With warm caches and prebuilt model variants with quantized weights, we've seen 50-200ms additional latency on typical medium models; big models can be higher.
[03:25] Liam: So for our interactive routes, 150ms p95 target, 200ms extra is risky. Can we keep hot standby in a proximate region?
[03:33] Priya: Yes — warm standby is the recommended pattern for strict latency SLOs: maintain a small reserved footprint in the standby region that stays warm. That increases cost but keeps latency low during failover. We can also do smart routing: keep critical routes pinned to Dedicated capacity in two regions if you want enterprise guarantees.

[04:00] Jordan: Customers often do hybrid — Dedicated in primary region + Hosted failover for secondary. That balances cost vs SLA. We provide instrumentation to estimate unit cost impact of failover in the Console.

[04:20] Maria: What's Redwood's SLA for Hosted endpoints? And for Dedicated? Any credits or uptime terms?
[04:27] Jordan: Hosted SLA is 99.9 (for commercial tier) historically, but we have enterprise SLA packages up to 99.95 with escalation and support. Dedicated has stricter SLAs — we can contract 99.95 or higher depending on commit and support tier. For Private we typically negotiate in the license terms with support SLAs.
[04:48] Ethan: Is the SLA per-region or global? If Hosted runs multi-region, is our SLA tied to a single region?
[04:55] Priya: SLA granularity is typically per-API endpoint/route as provisioned. If you provision dedicated pools in each region with cross-region routing, then the aggregate availability is a function of how you architect it; we'll provide guidance and runbooks.

[05:12] Liam: Audit/logging and encryption — our security team will require KMS integration and full request logs (redacted) for compliance. We also need SOC2 and ISO attestations. What do you provide?
[05:24] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated modes; Hosted can integrate with customer KMS for encrypt-at-rest depending on contract. We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 documentation and we can provide audited reports under NDA. Audit logs and request tracing are available in Console for Dedicated and Private; Hosted offers them as an add-on with configurable retention.

[05:55] Maria: Re: request logs — do logs contain prompt content? That's sensitive. We need option to not store prompts or mask PII.
[06:03] Priya: Yes — we have configurable retention and redaction policies. For Hosted we can do prompt redaction or opt-out of storing prompts. Private ensures data never leaves your VPC.

[06:20] Ethan: On the technical side — how do prefix caching and the KV cache behave across failovers? If primary loses state, does the secondary start cold?
[06:30] Priya: Cache is per-pool. There isn't an automatic global KV sync across regions because of consistency and latency. Patterns we recommend: 1) warm standby pools and a lightweight prefix-caching strategy to maintain high hit rates, 2) application-level sticky routing for sessions, and 3) pre-warm by replaying synthetic traffic before failing over. For very strict stateful workloads, Private deployment can run a shared cache backed by customer-managed storage, but that introduces complexity.
[07:05] Jordan: To add — we also support TTL-based cache warming and you can configure a proactive warming job via our API. It helps reduce cold-start impact during planned failover or upgrades.

[07:25] Maria: Do you offer multi-region active-active? We'd like active-active if possible to reduce failover pain.
[07:32] Priya: Redwood supports active-active at the routing layer — you can have pools in multiple regions receiving traffic. The complexity comes with KV cache consistency and session affinity; active-active works best for stateless or idempotent workloads. For stateful sessions we recommend active-passive with sticky sessions.

[08:00] Ethan: What's the observability surface? We need per-route latency, per-model KPIs, token-level cost breakdown, and traces that tie back to our request IDs.
[08:10] Priya: Console exposes per-route dashboards, token-level cost and latency, and tracing hooks where you can inject your request ID. We also provide logs and a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint for Dedicated/Private. Hosted can push metrics to customers' Datadog via integration.

[08:35] Liam: In a real incident, what's the escalation path? Who owns rollbacks?
[08:40] Jordan: We have an incident playbook. For Hosted incidents our ops team handles remediation; we run pre-agreed runbooks for failovers. For Dedicated there's joint ops: Redwood runbook + your on-call. For Private you manage the incident with Redwood support on standby per your SLA. We'll share runbooks as part of the POC.

[09:05] Maria: Pricing — switching to Dedicated or Private is a major cost. Can you give rough delta for keeping a warm standby in another region?
[09:13] Jordan: Ballpark: warm standby of a small dedicated pool can add 15-40% on top of primary capacity depending on utilization. Hosted failover is cheaper but variable in cost during incident as cross-region egress and higher per-token cost can spike. We'll produce a cost simulation once we have your traffic profile.

[09:40] Ethan: We also need to test a regional outage scenario. Can Redwood run a 24-hour benchmark with a traffic replay and failover exercise?
[09:48] Priya: Yes — we typically do a 24-48h benchmark with Canary and then a planned failover window. We'll need a sample traffic trace, a list of models/routes to include, and preferred failover timing. We can run the benchmark using your Dedicated pool and a Hosted fallback or Private if you want.

[10:10] Liam: For the benchmark, we need to measure cold-start percentiles, cache-warmup time, cost delta, and error profiles.
[10:16] Priya: We'll include those metrics and can instrument synthetic and real traffic. We'll also provide the raw benchmark data and a postmortem-style report with recommendations.

[10:30] Jordan: Quick vendor check — do you have an existing vendor?
[10:33] Maria: We're evaluating AWS SageMaker endpoints currently, and testing some self-managed Replicate/ONNX pipelines. We're keeping OpenAI for some generative tasks but want to standardize inference for low-latency features.
[10:44] Jordan: Got it. Redwood's angle is making this unified and operational — avoiding bespoke infra per model.

[11:00] Ethan: One thing from our SREs: cross-region egress costs are material for large token volumes. Can Redwood estimate egress cost in failover scenarios?
[11:10] Priya: We can estimate based on your traffic numbers; Console has a cost estimator and we can run hypothetical scenarios (failover to US, EU, etc.). For Dedicated, if you keep warm standby in the same cloud region family, egress can be lower. For Private, you control network egress policies.

[11:40] Maria: A question about model variants — we run trimmed quantized variants for latency. If primary runs int8 quantized and backup is fp16, do you retain quality consistency?
[11:50] Priya: We support model families and version mappings. During failover you can route to a compatible variant; quality differences are possible and you can set tolerance thresholds or annotate routes to prefer quality over latency. Part of the benchmark should include A/B checks for variants.

[12:15] Liam: Do you provide hooks for canary rollouts across regions? We do staged rollouts and want same tooling for multi-region deploys.
[12:22] Priya: Yes — Console supports canaries, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies with traffic weights. You can define region-aware rollout policies.

[12:40] Jordan: Let's cover an example failover policy: primary pool in eu-west-1 + standby in eu-central-1. Health checks fail over after 45s, sticky sessions prefer primary for 10 minutes, pre-warming job keeps top 10 prefixes cached in standby. We can show config examples.

[13:05] Maria: That sounds like what we want. Can you show a sample config and what the Console UI looks like?
[13:12] Priya: We'll share screenshots and the exact JSON/YAML of the routing policy. We'll include TTLs, health thresholds, and warming script.

[13:30] Ethan: Legal question — for Hosted failover where traffic crosses into US, we need to ensure PII that is EU-resident is not transferred unless we have consents. How do you handle quasi-residency flags per-route?
[13:40] Priya: You can tag routes and enforce hard-region constraints in policy. For EU-resident traffic you'd set a hard rule to only use EU pools; fallback would be blocked unless you explicitly enable cross-region for that route.

[14:00] Liam: If we need full control, Private is attractive but operational overhead is real. What are typical timelines for Private on-prem or VPC?
[14:08] Jordan: Typical Private VPC deployments are 6-8 weeks for standard sizes with our package; on-prem longer due to hardware procurement. Dedicated can be set up in 2-4 weeks depending on capacity. Hosted is immediate. We'll share a deployment timeline matrix.

[14:30] Maria: OK, next steps and dependencies? We'll need security review, procurement for a pilot, and an internal SRE slot for the benchmark window.
[14:38] Jordan: On our side, we'll share: 1) multi-region architecture doc and failover configs (Priya), 2) Dedicated vs Private pricing worksheet (Jordan), 3) SOC2/ISO artifacts under NDA. You'll share: 1) traffic profile and list of critical routes, 2) compliance checklist and target regions.

[15:05] Ethan: Anything else on monitoring during incident — do you support alerting ties into our PagerDuty?
[15:10] Priya: Yes — we integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, Datadog. We can forward alerts and provide runbook links in alerts.

[15:25] Maria: One last thing — what happens in a mid-deployment node failure for Dedicated? Auto-restarts or drain behavior?
[15:32] Priya: Dedicated pools have automatic instance replacement and rolling drain. We expose pool health and maintenance windows. You can opt into immediate failover or scheduled maintenance.

[15:50] Jordan: Alright, we'll recap in the follow-up email and attach the docs. Anything else?
[15:55] Liam: No, thanks. Looking forward to the architecture doc and cost projections.
[16:00] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone.

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-hearings in automated captioning; speakers sometimes overlap. Attached references mentioned: routing-policy-sample.yaml (link), pricing-dedicated-vs-private.xlsx (link), SOC2_artifact.pdf (NDA).

End of transcript.
